en: The eighth chapter:
Even by fate, when it suddenly brings about the objects desired by one's heart's wishes, it acts like a prior service rendered for the sake of the fortunate.
Association with wise people, the joy of seeing beloved kinsmen who were lost, and the acquisition of great jewels—what person would these not bring happiness in their home? (8.2)
Then, rising on the following day, the king departed from that village and entered the Vindhya forest. He wandered through it here and there for many days.

One day, as the monarch was wandering, he encountered the son of the forest-dwelling chieftain Śarabhaketu, named Vyāghraketu, who—somewhere along the way—had bound his high topknot upon his forehead with a coil of *śyāmalatā* creeper, dark as collyrium.

He was one who constantly bore upon the surface of his forehead—a region that seemed to be the very night itself accompanied by violence—a three-pronged frown born of no cause, which cast a darkness over it;
he was graced by an ear adorned with a glass-gem earring, made greenish by the luster of a single parrot’s wing used as an ornament;
and from his slightly squinting eye, with its sparse lashes, there flowed a natural radiance of passion like the blood of a hyena that had consumed an elixir.
With a sunken nose, a flattened lower lip,
a protruding chin, swollen jaws, and prominent cheekbones extending to the edges of the jaw, his neck was slightly bent forward at the base.
He had shoulders that reached halfway down his chest;
with his muscular chest— broadened by the harsh exertion of incessantly drawing his stiff, curved bow— he seemed to laugh at the vastness of the Vindhya mountain’s rocky slopes,
while with his pair of arms, as massive as pythons, he surpassed the length of the *śāla* trees on the snowy mountains.
He wore on his forearm— a forearm whose surface was made matted by small tufts of *nāgadamanī* grass entwined with the hair of boar cubs— a tin bracelet variegated with cow-tooth gems;
though not pot-bellied,

he appeared so due to his protruding belly, and he was encircled by a girdle of variously patterned leopard skins, studded with stars of tiger-skin patches and interlaced with a network of shriveled antelope hides.
His broad hips were gripped by a sword that gleamed from its horn-hilted, smooth handle and whose entire blade was smeared with a trace of quicksilver;
he possessed two massive thigh-staffs that seemed filled with flesh fallen away due to the effects of fresh youth;
and he wore a variegated tiger-skin garment fastened over a quiver made of bear-skin, which held a multitude of arrows mostly of the bhalla type.
He displayed a leanness that seemed to sprout forth from his quiver-adornment, which rested upon the curve of his back and was covered with hair as black as a swarm of bees;

on his left shoulder he bore a heavy bow made of *khadira* wood, its tip beautifully adorned with the feathers of a blue jay fixed to its upper third, its string fashioned from tough *tvacisāra* fibers, and its surface decorated with leafy patterns drawn in abundant peacock bile, while from his armpit hung a sharp arrow whose fletching was bound in a *svastika* pattern, one end of which had been inserted into a hole in a reed.

He was displaying, as if it were a handful of the very colors of the hunt, a hare whose nostrils were stained with streaks of blood as red as the *bandhūka* flower, its body exhibiting the whiteness of soft breast-hair clearly visible through its stretched skin; and a partridge with its neck knotted at the tip of a blade of *śitāṭanī* grass, its beak open and its copper-colored palate exposed.
With his right hand-tip occupied by Vikarṇa, whose face was defiled by foul poison like a black snake caught by its tail,
he resembled a moving tamāla tree on a mountain slope or a revolving pillar of solid iron wrought by a machine.
Moving like a fragment of collyrium stone being split off,
or like the very essence of iron melting from Mount Vindhya,
it was the consumption of pestilence for the herds of elephants.
He was the noose of Time for herds of deer,
the comet for the circles of lions,
and the Great Ninth Festival for the multitudes of buffaloes.
Like the very heart of violence,
like the fruit of evil,
like the cause of the Kali age.
Taking with him a young Śabara who was like the lover of the Night of Doom, he arrived;
and having stationed him at a distance, he made this representation:
"Your Majesty, there is a Śabara general named Bhūkampa, who is the lord of all this Vindhya range and the foremost among all the chiefs of the forest settlements."
"This man, named Nirghāta, is his sister's son; he is familiar even with the leaves of this entire Vindhya forest and wilderness, let alone its regions.
Let Your Majesty question him, for he is fit to carry out your command.
When this was said, Nirghāta bowed his head to the ground and made his salutation.
And he presented a gift of a hare along with a partridge;
the king, however, honoring him, asked him in person: "My good sir, are you familiar with this entire region?"
"And have you been dwelling in this manner during these days?
Has no woman of noble form come within the range of your sight, whether she belonged to the commander-in-chief or to some other subordinate of his?
Nirghāta, highly honored by the favor of the king’s address, bowed down.
Showing his respect, he addressed him: “Your Majesty,
even gold generally does not circulate here unguarded by the commander-in-chief, much less women.”
Nor is there any woman of such a form;
nevertheless, by the command of His Majesty, an effort is now being made every day to search for her, with no other duty at hand.

Furthermore, just half a *gavyūti* from here, in a great grove of trees growing at the foot of a mountain range—venerated by sages—there dwells a mendicant ascetic named Divākaramitra, a follower of Pārāśarya, surrounded by a large circle of disciples.
"He dwells near a mountain river;
perhaps he might find some news.
Having heard this, the king reflected: "For it is reported that from the venerable one whose name is auspiciously invoked, who has departed to heaven..."

"Grahavarman’s childhood friend, a learned Brāhmaṇa of the Maitrāyaṇīya school who had abandoned the triple Veda, attained meditative concentration in the Buddhist doctrine and took up the saffron robes while still a youth.
Generally, even seeing a friend produces great consolation for people.
Virtues are to be sought after by everyone;
who would not respect the state of a sage?
And the blessed life of renunciation brings dignity even to one who is dull-witted, for it is the home of the Dharma.
"How much more so, then, in the case of a wise person who captivates the minds of all people?

For this reason, our hearts have been constantly filled with curiosity regarding the sight of him; we see that this most auspicious encounter has occurred quite incidentally—a person whose sight was sought through diligent effort.
And he spoke aloud: "Aṅga!"
"Point out that place where that mendicant dwells.
Having spoken thus, he set out to go, following the path being shown by him.
Then, as he proceeded by degrees, there appeared *anavakeśin* trees with budding *karṇikāra* flowers.
There were abundant campaka trees with thick clusters of fruit, nameru trees weighed down by the burden of their harvest, groves of coconut palms with dark green leaves, groups of *nārikela* trees,
circles of *harikesara* and *sarala* trees, and rows of *kurabaka* shrubs bristling with a multitude of flower buds like horripilation.

The ten directions were being anointed with the loveliness of the red *aśoka* shoots; a beautiful grey hue was being produced by the spreading pollen of the blossoming *kesara* flowers; the *tilaka* and *tāla* trees were covered in their own pollen; and the *hiṅgu* plants were swaying.
Abounding in copious areca nuts,
with priyaṅgu trees tawny with their clusters of blossoms,
they bring joy to the people through the sweet humming of bees that gather into swarms upon the flower-clusters turned golden by pollen.
Where the itching of the temples of elephants was being relieved without hesitation by the trunks of *mucukunda* trees, dark with the pollen of their blossoms;
where the ground was made beautiful by lawns entirely covered by the young of black antelopes, leaping about fearlessly;
and where the sunlight was obscured by rows of *tamāla* trees, as black as the darkness itself.
The deodar trees were bristling with clusters of blossoms;
the avenues of *jambhīra* and *jambu* trees were overspread by a network of swaying betel-vine stems;
and the sky was kissed by circles of *dhūlīkadamba* flowers, white with the pollen of their blooms.

The ground was sprinkled with thick drops of honey; there was satisfaction for the dense sense of smell produced by the gathered fragrances; and the hollows of the *kuṭaja* trees had been turned into small incubators for a few days by the brooding hens.
Where the chatter of young sparrows was being carried on by the birds as they moved about, where the cakora birds were skillful in uttering cries with their mates, and where the ripe,
tawny pīlu fruits were being fearlessly devoured by numerous bhuruṇḍa birds;

Where the young fruits were stripped by parrots and birds that had been rendered fearless by the constant peeling of *sadāphala* and *kaṭphala* trees; where fawns of the hare rested comfortably upon stone slabs as tender as *śaileya* grass; and where swarms of monitor lizards rolled about with full confidence within the hollows of the roots of *śephālikā* shrubs.
Where herds of deer are free from fear, where flocks of mongooses sport without agitation, and where the growth of sprouts is swallowed by swarms of sweet-voiced cuckoos;
Herds of camari deer were chewing their cud in mango groves;
circles of blue water-fowl sat at their ease;
and young gavaya calves, having drunk their fill, were being watched by unchanging wolves.

The drumbeats of the flapping ears of herds of elephants— sluggish with the bliss of sleep induced by the sound of waterfalls on the mountain slopes nearby— were equaled only by the sweet melodies of the Kinnarīs singing close at hand;
the hyenas were exceedingly joyful,
and the snouts of young wild boars were stained with the green juice of turmeric rubbed upon their wounds.
Where jackals howl in the thickets of *guñjā* shrubs; where bracelets made of *jātīphala* nuts have fallen asleep upon *śālija* seeds;
and where swarms of young monkeys, provoked by their teeth, tear open the pouches of *pāṭala*-colored insects.
The *lavalī* creepers were being leaped upon by langurs greedy for *lakucha* fruit;
they had circles of sand-beds constructed as watering basins;
the currents of the mountain streams were diverted by rows of crooked water-jars; and water-pots were suspended from their thick trunks and branches.
The vine-arbors were adorned with begging bowls—suspended from their loops by sutra-strings and empty of alms; the forms of caityas were fashioned from *pāṭala* flowers near the huts;
and certain areas were stained by the decoction water used for dyeing the saffron-colored *cīvara* robes.
They were like clouds, filled with the clamor of flocks of peacocks;
they were like the Vedas, dense with the divisions of countless branches;
and they were like rubies, possessing great blue bodies.
They were like masses of darkness stealing the vision of all people's eyes,
like the Yamunā with its great lake raised high,
and like emerald-green pleasure-mountains of the spring season.
They were like mountains of collyrium sprouting new shoots,
like sons born of the Vindhya forest,
and like masses of the darkness of the netherworld that had burst through the earth and risen up.
Like recurring days of the rainy season,
like partial incarnations of the midnight hours of Kṛṣṇa,
they were like palaces made of sapphire belonging to the forest deities.
The trees descended into his field of vision ahead;
then it occurred to the king’s mind that the Bhadanta must surely be not far away.

Having dismounted and performed ablutions in a mountain stream, he [saw him] right there in this very place, where the thickets of the forest were deafened by the sound of neighing released simultaneously at the moment of resting.

Having halted at a spot and taking hold of his horse, he proceeded on foot alone, followed by only a few kings, with Mādhavagupta supporting him by the shoulder; with humility appropriate for the sight of ascetics in his heart and with his right hand, he set out.

Then, amidst those trees, he saw men from various lands—some leaning against trunks here and there, some seated upon rocky surfaces, and others inhabiting bowers of creepers within the forest thickets.
It was inhabited by those who had renounced passion, seated in the shade of the branches, dwelling at the roots of trees: Ārhatas, Maskarins,

Śvetapaṭas, Pāṇḍurabhikṣus, Bhāgavatas, Varnins, those who pluck out their hair, Kāpilas, Jainas, Lokāyatikas, followers of Kaṇāda, Upaniṣadic scholars, those who maintain God as the cause, Kāraṇḍhamins, Dharmaśāstrins, Paurāṇikas, and Sāptatantavas.

From afar, it was made known by those who had entered the state of discipleship— by grammarians, Pāñcarātrikas, and others, each listening to their own respective established doctrines, some being diligent scholars, some reflecting, some reciting, some doubting, some reaching certainty, some instructing, some disputing, some practicing, and some explaining.

Even by monkeys who were exceedingly well-disciplined, performing acts of devotion at the *caityas*, and devoted to the Three Refuges as supreme lay followers; by parrots skilled in the teaching of the Śākyas, instructing them on the treasury [of the Dharma]; by mainas characterized by the pacification of faults through the instruction of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*);
by mynas demonstrating the teachings of the Dharma; and even by owls who had grasped the light of wisdom through constant listening to the *jātaka* tales of the Bodhisattva.

He was being attended even by tigers whose natures had become cooled by the discipline born of their devotion to the Sugata, as they refrained from eating meat; and because many lion cubs sat confidently near his seat, he appeared like the supreme lord of sages seated upon a throne that was not artificial.
The tips of his feet were being licked by the tongues of wild deer as if they were drinking tranquility itself;
he was pleasing his beloved friend, Benevolence, with a young pigeon perched upon the palm of his left hand, feeding on wild rice like an ear-lotus;
and he created delusion among the people with the streaks of light from the nails of his other sprout-like hand.
With his neck outstretched, he was filling a cup made of emerald with streams of water like a peacock;
here and there, he was scattering grains of śyāmāka rice by himself for rows of ants;
and he was wrapped in a very soft, reddish-brown monastic robe.
He seemed to anoint the eastern quarter of the sky with the thick glow of the morning sun;
with the radiance of his body—pale red and resembling the luster of a polished ruby—he appeared to be instructing even the quarters of the world in the adoption of the saffron robe.

Out of humility, he cast his eyes downward like a cluster of gently budding white water-lilies; they were glossy, white, and serene, raining down what seemed like nectar for the sake of reviving the tiny creatures crushed by the feet of men.
He was as if fashioned from the very atoms of every scriptural syllable;
though supremely devoted to the Sugata,
he was fixed in his ascetic penance without wavering.
Like light, it illuminates all things as they truly exist for those seeking vision; it is worthy of being approached even by a Sugata,
and as if worthy of being propitiated even by the Dharma of the Avadhi.
He was, as it were, worthy of being gladdened even by gladness itself; worthy of being honored even by honor itself; and worthy of being saluted even by the very state of being saluted.
It was as if it were desirable even to the Self, as if it were the object of meditation even for meditation,
and as if it were the object of knowledge even for knowledge.
He is the birth of recitation,
the rim of restraint,
and the essence of austerity.
The body is the vessel of purity, the treasury of virtue,
and the abode of trust.
Good conduct is the very essence of virtuous behavior;
all possessions are the essence of omniscience; and skillfulness is the essence of courtesy.
He saw Divākaramitra, who had reached the further shore of compassion for others and the bliss of nirvāṇa, and who was now in the middle stage of his life.

Inspired by a profound respect for his exceedingly peaceful and majestic appearance, Divākaramitra paid him homage from afar with reverence, bowing his head, speaking words, and directing his mind toward him.

For Divākaramitra was by nature filled with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and he was especially moved by that extraordinary, non-ordinary appearance of the king— an aspect never seen before, worthy of the supramundane realm, all-surpassing, radiant with the full majesty of great power, and resplendent.
Delighted by his profound courtesy, which was both weighty and illuminating of his noble lineage, he was simultaneously captivated in both eye and mind;

and though of a steadfast nature, he rose with hurried respect, gathered the hem of his monastic robe— which was hanging down and swaying slightly from his left shoulder— with a small upward motion, and extended his right hand, which was skilled in the initiation of granting manifold assurances of safety.

He favored the king with words that were affectionate and sweet, marked by the lines of the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), and by the respectful gift of health. And he greeted him with words of welcome, honoring him as if he were a venerable teacher who had arrived; he invited him to sit upon his own seat, saying, "Please be seated here. Then he spoke to the disciple standing at his side: "O long-lived one..."
"Bring water for his feet in your water-pot," he said.

The king, however, thought to himself: "The nobility of the well-born is indeed a bond of restraint that is not made of iron. It is only fitting that the venerable Grahavarman, who is so fond of virtue, has described this man's qualities so many times."
And he spoke aloud: "O Blessed One, for me who am favored by the merit of beholding you, this favor bestowed by your honor appears as if it were redundant;
and for one already accepted through the gracious clarity of your vision, these efforts of offering hospitality such as a seat seem like a mere formality.

For one such as you, the very ground is a superlative seat; conversing before you is like a ceremonial sprinkling of nectar that has washed away every part of my body, so that even a localized function [like offering water] would be redundant.
Even the water for washing the feet is useless.
Please remain as you please.
Having said, "I shall sit," he sat down right upon the ground.

Considering that "in truth, for those who possess power, the supreme ornament is an excess of humility, whereas jewels and the like are merely a burden of stone," the Venerable One, though repeatedly entreated by the King, did not comply with his words; instead, he once again took his own seat.
Having stood for a certain moment with his heart rendered motionless by the fetters of his pair of steady eyes fixed upon the lotus-face of the king,

he spoke to the forest of creepers— which was white with clusters of blooming flowers and fragrant with the scent arising from the consumption of roots and fruits— as if washing away the impurity of the Kali age with the stainless rays of his teeth: "From this day forward, not only is this [king] beyond reproach..."
Even this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), though worthy of worship, has its true essence revealed;
for what wonder indeed is not beheld by those who live, when such an inconceivable form as this comes before the path of their vision?
By means of such experiences, people infer the meritorious deeds performed in previous births through the festivals of their hearts.
Even in this life, the fruit of our penance— so difficult to behold— has been granted by him who shows us the Beloved of the Gods;
with our two eyes, we have drunk nectar to satiety,
and our mind has become free from longing for the bliss of liberation.
Without great merits, eyes do not rest upon a virtuous person such as you.
That is a truly auspicious day on which you were born;
that is a well-born mother who gave birth to you, O long-lived one, the source of life for the entire world of living beings.

Meritorious indeed are those merits of which you are the fruition; those atoms of well-performed austerity constitute every limb embraced by you. It is because of this that you have come to possess such auspiciousness and good fortune.
That state of being a man is truly blessed which remains steadfast;
for indeed, even though I am one seeking liberation, having beheld this fortunate being, faith has arisen in me once more toward human birth.
Even by us who do not desire it, the flower-armed god [Kāma] has been seen.
Today the eyes of the forest deities have achieved their purpose;
today the birth of these trees has become fruitful, since you have come within their range. The sweetness of your nectar-like words must surely be experienced.
Even when reflecting upon it, I do not find anyone on earth who could have been the preceptor of such discipline in your childhood.
In every way, the multitude of virtues was absent while the long-lived one was yet unborn.
Blessed is that monarch in whose lineage you have arisen like a pearl made of pure luster.
Our minds are thus agitated by the thought: "How may we perform a service pleasing to such a meritorious person who has somehow arrived here?
What are we, compared to the roots, tubers, and fruits that sustain the entire host of forest-dwellers, or the waters of the mountain streams?
This wretched body of ours is intended solely for the benefit of others."
My entire remaining property is for the hospitality of dear guests;
as for the few drops of knowledge that remain under my own control,
affection does not consider their utility.
And if it does not obstruct any minor task that must be protected, or any syllable that ought to be spoken, then may you speak; for our hearts long to hear all of this.

By what burden of duty has your noble self adorned this land, which is unfit for wandering mendicants? And how long will this hardship of wandering through the empty wilderness continue for you, O heap of auspiciousness?
"And why does this body of yours appear as if scorched, though it is clearly undeserving of such torment?

The king, however, replied with even greater reverence: "Noble sir, by your very speech—which shows such concern, which pours forth a stream of sweetness like nectar, and which constantly bestows support to my heart—you have already accomplished everything."
"I am fortunate that you, who are worthy of honor, consider me worthy of respect even though I am one who should not be approached with such formalities.
And let your wise mind take note of the cause of this hardship of wandering through the great forest.
For me, whose entire circle of beloved kinsmen has perished, there remains but one bond to my life: my youngest sister."
She too, wandering due to separation from her husband and out of fear of defeat by her enemies, somehow reached this Vindhya forest,
which is teeming with the forces of inauspicious Śabaras and thick with herds of elephants that have been disregarded.
It was a place where there was constant fear of countless lions and śarabhas, where the paths of travelers were lost due to the presence of vast buffaloes,
and which was filled with extremely sharp arrows, kusha grass, and axes.
"He entered a place as treacherous as a hundred pits;

therefore, we wander incessantly through this forest day and night to search for her, yet we do not find her. May the Guru also tell us if, perhaps, some news of her has reached his ears from anyone wandering in the woods."
Then, having heard that, the Venerable One, as if seized by agitation, spoke again: "O wise one!
Indeed, no such event has ever come to us;
for we are unworthy recipients of such pleasant tidings and gifts from you."

While he was thus meditating, a certain monk, who appeared to be in the prime of his life, suddenly approached from another direction; looking as if agitated, with palms joined before him, filled with compassion and eyes brimming with tears, he spoke: “Venerable Sir, Reverend One!
A great tragedy is unfolding.”
And she, though formerly of auspicious form, now being but a child overwhelmed by powerful calamity, has entered the fire, helpless under the onset of grief for her husband;
may the Blessed One show honor to her whose life has departed,
and may he assist her with appropriate consolations.
"Even one who has never before ceased from being like a mere worm or insect, when fallen into the range of vision of this noble one—a mass of compassion—he becomes one who suffers.

But the king, feeling a sense of rivalry born of his own status, yet melting inwardly with brotherly affection, his heart tormented by grief, somehow managing to speak with a throat seized by stammering, his voice faltering and his eyes welling with tears, he asked: "O Parāśarī, how far away is that woman of such a kind, and for how long has she been wandering thus?"
Or were you asked, O blessed lady: "Who are you? To whom do you belong? From where have you come?"
"For what purpose have you come to this forest, and for what reason do you enter the fire?
I wish to hear everything told from the beginning: how did you come within the range of my noble brother's sight, and of what appearance was he?"

Thus addressed by the king, the mendicant replied: "O noble one, listen. This very morning, having paid my respects to the Blessed One, I wandered at will for a great distance along this riverbank, which is so soft with its sand.
And in a thicket of forest creepers near a mountain stream, I heard a sound like that of female bees distressed by a frost-stricken lotus pond."

I heard the women’s wailing, which was as incessant and piercing as the sound of the strings of a lute being played out of tune; it was a continuous, heart-rending cry that filled me with distress. Feeling compassion arise within me, I went to that place.

And I saw [a man] whose fingers were dripping with blood from being bitten by lizards; whose eyes were narrowed by the agony of arrow-shards and splinters lodged in his heels; whose feet were motionless due to swelling from the fatigue of the road; whose ankles were bound with birch bark because of the pain from wounds on tree stumps; who suffered from a fever arising in his calves from the exhaustion of lameness caused by wind-disorder (vātakuṇḍa); whose hair was as pale as dust; and whose knees were worn away by the matted locks of a *kharjūra* plant.

And she was one whose thighs were torn by *śatāvarī* creepers; whose fine silk garment was rent by the sharp points of thorns on the branches of tall bamboo thickets; whose delicate palms and belly were scratched by the bristly nets of *badarī* vines hanging down in their longing for fruit; whose arms were exhausted by roots, tubers, and fruits dug up with deer-horns; and whose mouth was parched by the absence of betel and broken by bits of tender *āmalakī* fruit.

Some carried red lotuses and *kuśa* grass; some had their eyes swollen and smeared with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*); one held a *kaṇṭakī* branch with its leaves serving as a parasol; another fanned him with a plantain leaf; another bore water in a vessel made from a lotus leaf; another carried a bundle of lotus stalks as provisions for the journey; and another held a coconut-shell jar filled with pine oil, suspended from the hem of his fine Chinese silk garment.

She was surrounded by a dense circle of women— mute, hunchbacked, dwarfed, deaf, and barbarian— who were rendered speechless and distressed by their lingering grief; she, whose innate splendor was not abandoned even in this time of calamity,
and whose body was being veiled within by the fresh sprouts of nearby forest creepers reflected upon her, as if those tender shoots were the wounds of sorrow forming a pall over her.
Her feet were reddened by blood dripping from wounds inflicted by the sharp sprouts of *darbha* grass, as if by lac-dye applied during her pursuit;
she bore a face that, though shaded by a lotus leaf held by one of the women—its stalk raised upward—was nonetheless lusterless;
and she surpassed even the sky in its extreme emptiness.
She was like one made of clay due to her lack of consciousness, like one made of air due to the abundance of her sighs, like one made of fire due to the continuity of her burning heat,
like one made of water due to the flow of her tears, like one made of the sky due to her lack of support, like one made of lightning due to her flickering restlessness,
and like one made of sound due to the profusion of her lamentations; she had cast off her pearl necklaces, silken garments, jeweled flowers, and golden leaf-ornaments.
Like a wish-fulfilling creeper fallen in a great forest,
her limbs tenderized by falling upon the head of the Supreme Lord, she was like the Gaṅgā descended to earth,
with the sprouts of her feet greyed by the pollen of forest flowers.
Like the form of the moon at dawn longing for another world,
she was like a lotus-stalk of the Mandākinī withering away, its beauty of white eyes revealed and distressed by the release of its own water;
like a night-lily with eyes closed in exhaustion from the touch of the unbearable rays of the sun, she spent the day in sorrow.
With her body so emaciated that it resembled the flame of a lamp at dawn betrayed by its burnt wick,
and with her pale form requiring protection from the elephants stationed at her side, she was like a forest elephant submerged in a great lake;
she had entered both the dense forest and deep meditation.

She stood at the foot of a tree and yet was fallen into death; she was held in the lap of her nurse and yet was cast into great misfortune; she was distanced from her husband and yet was joined with happiness;
she was purged by wandering and yet was restored to her life.
Distressed by her mass of hair and by the means of death; discolored by the dust of the road and by bodily pains;
and scorched by the fierce heat of the sun and by widowhood.
She held her face with her hand and maintained silence;
she was embraced by her dear friends and by grief; likewise, she was abandoned by her kinsmen and by her amorous graces.
With her pair of ears and her own self liberated;
with her ornaments and all worldly undertakings abandoned;
and with her bracelets and her desires shattered.
With female attendants clinging to her feet with needle-like blades of darbha grass, and with her beloved fixed upon her heart with his gaze;
With long sobs of grief and disheveled hair, with emaciated bodies and exhausted merit, they fell at her feet with aged forms and flowing streams of tears,
accompanied by a meager remnant of attendants and life.
She was languid in her opening of the eyes, skillful in shedding tears,
and constant in her anxieties.
Her hopes were severed; she was emaciated in body,
yet heavy in her sighing.
Filled with suffering,
empty of sentient beings,
and presided over by exhaustion.
Empty by reason of her heart, motionless by reason of her resolve, yet trembling from her fortitude.
Moreover, it is the dwelling place of calamities, the receptacle of anxieties,
and the abode of instabilities.
The foundation of misfortunes,
the dwelling place of dejections,
the haunt of calamities.
The object of misfortune for the unfortunate, the cause of agitation for those who are agitated, and the source of compassion.
I had considered that women are beyond the reach of dependence on others,
and I thought it strange that even such a form as this should be touched by afflictions;
yet, when I drew near, she, despite her condition, bowed with great respect and her head inclined low.
But I, impelled by powerful compassion and desiring to address her, again reflected in my mind: "How indeed shall I address this noble lady?
To call her 'Child' is too familiar; to call her 'Mother' is too flattering."
“Sister” is self-aggrandizement;
“Queen” is the address of attendants;
“Princess” is indistinct.
“Laywoman” implies a mere wish;
“mistress” implies the acceptance of the status of a servant;
“lady” is appropriate for other women.
"O long-lived one" is unpleasant at this stage;
"O auspicious lady" is contradictory in this condition;
"O moon-faced one" is contrary to the opinion of the wise.
“Child” implies a lack of respect;
“Noble Lady” implies the imposition of old age; “Virtuous One” implies a result contrary to reality;
“Madam” is a term common to all.
Moreover, "Who are you? is an unrefined question;
"Why do you weep? causes one to remember the cause of suffering; and "Do not weep" is not fitting as long as the cause of grief has not been removed.
On what basis do you say “be comforted,” when the welcome is stale and the inquiry “are you sitting at ease” is a mere formality?

While I was thus reflecting, a certain woman from that group of women rose up; appearing noble in form yet overwhelmed by grief, she approached me, bowed her head—spotted with a few grey hairs—and pressed it to the ground. Scorching my feet with teardrops that indicated the incomparable agony of her heart, she spoke to my very core with most piteous words: "O Blessed One!..."

The life of renunciation is generally characterized by compassion for all sentient beings; moreover, the followers of the Sugata are skilled in the initiatory rites for exhausting the suffering of those who have entered the path.
And the teaching of the Blessed One Śākyamuni is the ancestral home of compassion.
The Jaina nature of the virtuous is ever-ready to benefit all people;
and the dharma of the sages is the means for accomplishing the next world.
Furthermore, no accumulation of merit greater than the protection of living beings is proclaimed by the people in this world.
Young women are compassionate by their very nature, how much more so when overcome by calamity? And virtuous people are a field of success for the words of those in distress;

for this mistress of ours, due to the death of her father, the absence of her husband, the exile of her brother, and the loss of the rest of her circle of kinsmen, possesses an exceedingly tender heart and is childless.

Her pride was wounded by the humiliation inflicted by her lowly husband, and her natural spirit was further distressed by the hardships of wandering through this great forest; thus, her heart was rendered utterly weak by these manifold calamities, one after another, brought about by cursed fate.

Unable to endure such terrible suffering, disregarding even her elders—who had previously been honored by her even in dreams—as she seeks to dissuade him; setting aside her unbroken affection even during jests, and ignoring her dear friends; she enters the fire, utterly despising with her mind this man who was never before treated with contempt, who is now pleading for mercy, helpless and protectorless, his eyes clouded with tears, and who has disregarded even his circle of servants.
"May he protect us!

May even the Noble One exert his voice, which is purified by the instruction of means for removing immeasurable sorrow, upon her," she said most piteously. Raising me up while being even more distressed, he spoke softly: "Noble Lady, it is just as you say."
This grief of this woman of meritorious intent is beyond the scope of our words; yet, if she can be saved for even a single moment, this request of mine will not be in vain,
for my teacher, like another Blessed Sugata, is indeed present nearby.
"When this account has been told by me, the supremely compassionate one will certainly come;

and with his own well-spoken words of the Sugata, which pierce through the veil of the darkness of suffering, and with his skill in speech— weighty with various scriptures and illustrated by apt examples— he will lead this woman of virtuous conduct to the path of awakening."
Having heard that, she fell at his feet once more, saying, "May the noble one hasten!
Then I, approaching in haste, reported this distressing occurrence—this most piteous death of many young women who were helpless and wretched—to your majesty, my preceptor.
Thereupon, the king, having understood the monk's words, though he had not yet heard his sister’s name, was filled with tears.

His mind humbled by a grief that corresponded in every aspect to his outward appearance, and his doubts dispelled by the very sight [of her], he felt as if burnt within his ears upon hearing of his sister’s condition;

then he spoke to the Śramaṇa teacher: “Noble sir, this must surely be that very same sister of mine—this ignoble person, whose heart is exceedingly hard, who is most cruel, and who is so unfortunate.”
"Destined by fortune to be led to this state by those who are enemies without cause, this wretched woman informs me thus through my very heart as it tears apart.
Having said this, she also addressed that ascetic: "Noble sir, arise!
Show me where she is!"
"Exert yourself to acquire the merit of saving many lives; let us go, if by some means we may find her still alive," he said, and as he spoke, he rose up.
Then the Teacher, followed by his entire circle of disciples, dismounted from his horse along with the whole assembly of local nobles.

Followed by a troop of cavalry drawing up from behind, and with the son of the Śākyas showing him the way ahead, he proceeded on foot toward that place, as if drinking it in with his eyes at every step through the dense intervals.

Gradually approaching, he heard from within the thicket of creepers the various kinds of cries appropriate to the moment uttered by a great group of women who were about to die: “O Blessed Dharma!... ”
Run quickly!
O family deity,
O Goddess Dharaṇī!

Why do you not comfort your grieving daughter? Where indeed has the prosperity of the Puṣpabhūti household gone into exile? O Protector, why do you not awaken this widow, your wife, who is now helpless, tormented by various afflictions caused by the power of her husband’s words?
O Blessed One, O Sugata, while your devotees are burning with distress, you are asleep! O you who favor the abode of King Dharmapuṣpabhūti,
how is it that you have become indifferent?
O Vindhya, friend in adversity, even to you this joining of palms is in vain;
O Mother Great Forest!
O Pataṅga, do you not hear her crying out as she falls into your path? Be gracious and protect this helpless woman devoted to her husband!
O you who are protected by effort, you ungrateful outcaste of character,
do you not protect the princess? Was she not recognized by her auspicious marks?
"Alas, Queen Yaśomatī, composed of love for your daughter! You have been crushed by this wretched, fire-brand of a demon.
O King, you do not rush to the aid of your daughter while she is being consumed!"
O Pratāpaśīla,
your affection for your child has become slackened;
O Great King Rājyavardhana!
"You do not run; your sisterly affection has grown cold!
Oh, how cruel is the nature of a hungry ghost!
Begone, O wicked fire, you who are merciless in the slaughter of women!"
You do not feel shame while burning!
O brother Vāta,
I am your slave.
Quickly report the burning of the Queen to the God, the joy who removes the suffering of afflicted beings!
O you who are utterly devoid of compassion, you outcaste of grief, your desire is fulfilled!
O demon of separation, you giver of pain!
You are content!
In this lonely forest, whom shall I cry out to? To whom shall I speak? To whom shall I go for refuge?
Which direction shall I go? What shall I do, unfortunate as I am,
O Gāndhārikā?
This vine-noose has been seized!
O Piśācī Mocanikā, release this quarrel over grasping the branch!
O kalahamsi, you strike; what head could be higher than this? O Mangalika, why do you still weep with unrestrained throat even now?
"O beautiful one, the company of friends is departing.
O Śabarikā, how will you remain in this inauspicious camp of corpses? O slender-limbed Mālavatī, delicate as a lotus stalk, you too shall fall into the fire. "I am weary."
Mother Mātaṅgikā,
you too have accepted death.
Child Vatsikā!
How will you dwell in this city of the dead, which is so undesired? O Nāgarikā, you have attained greatness through this devotion to your master.
O Virājakī, you are truly radiant because of your resolve to sacrifice your life in the calamity of the princess.
O bearer of the water-pot, you who are well-acquainted with the resolve to leap from the Bhṛgu cliff, you are blessed!
O Ketakī, where else could there be such a good mistress even in a dream?
O Menakā, may the God, while burning away the God of Love, grant me the very service of the Goddess in birth after birth!
"Victory! O Vijayā, fan the fire!
Sānumatī, Indīvarikā bows to you; she wishes to go to heaven. Kāmadāsī, grant me the space to circumambulate the fire!"
O Vicārikā, prepare the fire;
O Kirātikā, scatter a profusion of flowers.
Kurārī, prepare the funeral pyre strewn with *kurubaka* buds!
Cāmara, take up the yak-tail fan!
And once more, O Narmadā, you must endure these boundless, playful laughs fashioned in jest upon my neck.
O auspicious Subhadrā, may your journey to the next world be auspicious;
O village girl who takes delight in virtues that are beyond the reach of the common folk!
Go to a happy rebirth!
Vasantikā, grant me an interval!
The queen’s parasol-bearer takes her leave.
Cast your gaze!
Your beloved Vijayasenā is giving up her life;
here is that very Muktikā, the stage-director of the drama, wailing aloud nearby.
"O Princess, your esteemed betel-bearer Patralatā falls at your feet!
O Kaliṅgasenā,
this is the final embrace."

Press me tightly with your breast! My life-breaths are departing, Vasantasenā! Mañjulikā, how many times have you wiped this eye of mine, which is smeared with the blood of thousands of most unbearable sorrows?
Why do you weep so much while embracing me? Such a transformation is common, O Yaśodhanā;
why do you still try to comfort me, Mādhavikā?
To what state have these conciliations reached?
O Kālindī, the time for the entreaties and folded hands of our friends has passed.
O Unmattikā, O Mattapālikā,
you have disregarded the entreaties of your beloveds;
O Cakoravatī, loosen [your hold].
O grasping lotus, take my hand! O Kamalini, what is the use of this repeated reproaching of fate?
For a long time, the pleasure of union with your friends has not been attained.
Noble Mahattarikā Taraṅgasenā,
salutations!
Friend Saudāminī, you have been seen!
O Havyavāhana, bring the unblown flowers; O Kamudikā, give me the *acana* flowers; O Rohiṇī, lend me the support of your hand for my ascent upon the funeral pyre.
Mother, nurse,
be steadfast;
such indeed are the ripenings of the karmas of those who have committed evil deeds.
This is a salutation with joined palms to the feet of the Noble Ones;
this, O Mother, is my final prostration as I depart for the next world.
Why, Lavalikā, at the time of death?
This tumultuous joy, full of bliss, is overwhelming my heart; why are my limbs bristling with horripilation and trembling?
Vāmanikā, my left eye is throbbing.
"O friend crow,
you cry out in vain at every moment before this milky tree;
to the north, there is the neighing of horses, like that of a doe."
"Kuraṅgikā, whose is this lofty parasol that shines here between the trees?
It is discerned;
by whom has the name of the Noble One—whose name is well-grasped—been uttered, for it is as if made of nectar?"
"O Queen, congratulations on this great festival of the arrival of King Harṣa!
Having heard this, he approached in haste and beheld Rājyaśrī, who was fainting and intent on entering the fire.
And he anxiously supported her forehead with his hand as she lay there with eyes closed in a swoon;
then, from the medicinal herbs bound upon the wrist of that beloved brother, he— as if distilling the essence of their potency capable of restoring life,
as if vomiting forth the inconceivable power of the jewels of his bracelets, and as if pouring out nectar with the moonbeams of his fingernails— [acted].

As if binding upon her head the moonstone crest-jewel dripping with cool spray from the rising moon, and as if extinguishing her burning heart with an exceedingly cold finger made of lotus-stalks, Rājyaśrī suddenly opened her eyes at the gladdening touch of a hand that seemed to bring her life back from somewhere.
And so, having suddenly embraced her brother— who had arrived unexpectedly, whose sight was unimagined, and who was like a vision seen in a dream— she,
overwhelmed by a mass of grief that manifested at that very moment and pervaded her entire being,
poured forth a thick torrent of tears from her eyes as if through two channels at the mouth of a river, crying out, "O Father!"
Crying out, "O mother! O friends!",
and having wailed for a very long time with a loud voice— her grief intensified by the weight of her genuine sisterly affection—
she was consoled by her brother, who covered her face with his hand, saying, "Child, be steadfast."
"O auspicious lady,
carry out the word of your elder brother and guru," thus was she entreated by the teacher,
O Queen.
"Do you not see the condition of the King? Enough of this excessive weeping," she was thus entreated by the royal attendants, yet [she replied],
"My Lord..."

Although she was being entreated by her attendants, "Look after your brother," and although she was being restrained by the elder female relatives, saying, "Daughter, rest first; you must cry out again later," she [continued].
“Dear friend, why do you weep? Remain silent.”
"O King, she is suffering intensely," though thus entreated by her friends,
she— her throat constricted by a flood of tears that burst forth from the weight of many long-accumulated and unbearable sorrows,
and her inner heart filled with a vast burden of grief— wailed piteously for some time in a loud, drawn-out voice.
When the force of his anger had subsided, his brother drew him away from the vicinity of the fire and, leading him to the foot of a nearby tree, sat down.

The teacher, gradually perceiving that it was indeed Harsha, felt his respect increase all the more; having passed about a moment with even greater attentiveness, he himself took water brought by a disciple who had been signaled discreetly, and bowing low, offered lotus leaves for the washing of the face.

The lord of men also, having respectfully taken her hand, first washed his sister’s eye—which was copper-red from incessant weeping and streaming with a long-accumulated flood of tears like a red lotus—from which he afterwards washed his own.
When the king had thus washed his moon-like face, the entire assembly became silent on all sides, as if painted in a picture.
Then the lord of men spoke very softly to his sister: “Child!”
"Pay homage to this venerable and noble sir;

he is the second heart of your husband and our own preceptor. At these words of the king, as the princess bowed with tears flowing once more—her eyes opened by the mention of her husband's acquaintance—the teacher [spoke].
With eyes moistened by a firmness that was breaking under the weight of a flood of tears—tears that had been suppressed with great effort—he turned his gaze away slightly and sighed deeply.
Smiling for a moment and displaying courtesy, the soft-spoken youth addressed him in a sweet voice: “O heap of auspiciousness!”
Enough of weeping for so long;
the world of kings has not yet ceased its wailing.
Let the necessary rite of bathing be performed.
"Having bathed, you must go back to that very same land.

Then the king, following both worldly custom and the command of his preceptor, rose, bathed in the mountain river along with his sister, and returned to that very spot. There, having first fixed his attention upon her, he, standing by her side, caused his elder sister—who was surrounded by her attendants and overcome with grief—to eat; she had accepted the means of sustenance only through the effort shown by the presentation of her husband's funeral cakes.
Immediately thereafter, he himself took up his sustenance through food;

and having eaten, he related in detail to his sister, from the time of her imprisonment, the agitation caused by the Gaudas at Kanyakubja, her secret escape under the protection of a nobleman named Gupta, and her hearing of the news of Rājyavardhana’s death upon her departure.

From her attendants, he heard the entire account: how she had rejected food, how she was overcome by the lack of nourishment, how she had become weary from wandering through the Vindhya forest, how she had conceived a sense of renunciation, and how she had begun to enter the alms-bowl.
Then, as the king sat comfortably at the foot of a tree on a secluded spot accompanied by his sister, with his followers standing at a distance, the teacher approached and slowly sat down beside him.
After remaining silent for a short while, he began to speak briefly: "O Illustrious One, listen!
We have something to relate—this man, out of the madness of youth, having disregarded his many wives who were exceedingly fickle due to their own entry into youth, [became like] the king of stars..."
In former times, Rājanīkarṇapūra, being excessively fickle, abducted Tārā— the lawful wife and consort of Dhiṣaṇa, the domestic priest of Puruhūta—
and fled from heaven.
Sporting with her, whose eyes were like those of a startled cakora bird, who was full of passion for him, and who was delightful in every aspect, he wandered through beautiful lands.
And after a long time, with great difficulty and out of respect for the speech of all the gods, he finally returned that [ring] to the Lord of Speech;
yet, in his heart, he burned incessantly from the fireless fire of separation from that fair-hipped woman.
Once, however, feeling distressed, he beheld his own reflection cast upon the clear waters of the ocean from the mountain of sunrise.
Having seen that, he was suddenly reminded of Tārā’s face with its smiling cheeks;

his mind agitated by the madness of love, though dwelling in heaven, he became ill at ease and shed large drops of tear-water from his eyes, which were as white as the radiance of a full-blown cluster of night-lotuses.

Then, as they were falling, pearl-oysters swallowed them all together in the ocean; and within the cavities of their bellies, those pearls became transformed into pearls. There, Vāsuki by name, the lord of the poison-spitting serpents and a dweller of the netherworld (rasātala), somehow obtained them. With those pearls, which displayed a multitude of stars even at the bottom of the netherworld, he fashioned a single-string necklace.
And he gave her the name Mandākinī.

By the power of the Blessed Soma, the lord of all medicinal herbs, and because she was born from snow and nectar, she became a complete destroyer of poisons and a remover of the suffering of all sentient beings through her mere touch;
for which reason Vāsuki always wore her upon himself to pacify the heat of his venom.

After some time had passed, once upon a time, a monk named Nāgārjuna—who was brought from that king of nāgas to the depths of the netherworld by the nāgas themselves—begged for and obtained a single-string necklace.
Having emerged from the subterranean realm, he gave it to his friend, the sovereign of the three oceans and lord of men named Sātavāhana.
And in the course of time, through a succession of disciples, it somehow came into our hands.
"Even though this adopted courtesy may seem like a slight to those such as you,

nevertheless, let your long-lived self— who, perceiving all beings with the intellect of a physician, is engaged in protecting the mass of all creatures— accept this single-string necklace, Mandākinī, which is tied to the edge of the robe of the monk standing nearby, out of regard for protection against poison," he said, and released it.

Even as she was being released, her vast circle of rays— smeared with luster, expansive, and spreading forth with clear brilliance— suddenly flooded the quarters of the sky with whiteness; at that moment, the trees seemed to blossom from their very roots out of longing for the budding creepers shaken by her departure,
while the flocks of swans from the forest lakes rushed toward her, white with the flapping of their wings, as if greedily pursuing fresh lotus stalks.

The landscape appeared as if it were bursting open with groves of *ketakī* flowers, white with dust crumbling under the weight of their own mass and pure with the clusters of stamens revealed by the splitting of their bellies;
it seemed awakened by lilies with jagged petals fully unfurled;
and it was as if stirred by herds of lions, whose manes were like flashes of lightning filling the circle of the quarters.
The forest seemed to be laughing, as the groves were being painted white by the light of the rays from the teeth of its smiling blossoms;
it seemed to have burst into bloom, with the *kāśa* thickets unrestrainedly laughing through their loosened buds and filaments;
and it seemed to be whirling about, as the herds of yaks appeared white with the circles of their young tails spinning in agitation.
The day was as if washed by the mountain river’s flood, which surged forth with swelling, frothy, and most tremulous waves;
it was as if illuminated by the risen full moon, whose circle of blossoming rays filled the quarters of the sky out of delight at the sight of the rival stars;
and it was as if cleansed of the dust that had greyed the horizons during the forest fire.
The faces of the women, though washed as if anew, were still marred by tears;

yet the king, his eyes repeatedly opening and closing as they were overwhelmed by her thick, radiant beams, finally beheld— with great effort— that sight which fulfills all hopes, appearing like a mass of spray from the trunks of the world-elephants arrayed in a row.
It was like the autumn moonlight released from the clouds and drawn into a streak;
like the path of the young crescent moon made visible by the marks of its footprints; like the garland of the Seven Sages (the Great Bear) set free from their hands as they became motionless;
and like a digit of the moon belonging to Śiva, whose power and splendor surpassed all the ornaments of the world.

Like the radiance of the ocean of milk emerged and embraced by the quality of whiteness; like the Gaṅgā, which relieves distress and has descended through a succession of many great mountain ranges; like a vanguard banner of the arrival of Maheśvara’s state, with its shimmering, flickering silken cloth constantly quivering;
and like the row of teeth of the approaching Lord, white with the essence of ivory.
She was like a self-chosen garland of the Fortune of the World, capable of fulfilling the most excellent desires;
she was like the playful smile of the Earth, difficult to perceive because it was shielded by her own sprout-like hands;
and she was like the rosary of the Kingly Duty, which had begun the practice of incantations and the treasury of secret counsel.
Beholding this [tablet], which was like an ornament to the ocean and resembled a ledger for the treasury of Kubera,
he was filled with wonder in his mind for a long time;
the teacher, however, having lifted it up, fastened it upon the king’s graceful shoulder.
Then the king, showing his pleasure in return, replied: “Noble sir, men are generally unworthy of such jewels as these.
This must be either the perfection of your asceticism or the grace of the gods.”
And what are we now, whether regarding our own selves, let alone our acceptance or rejection?
From the moment we first saw him, our hearts have been captivated by the multitude of his noble qualities, and we are no longer masters of ourselves.
We have resolved that this body shall be for the service of the Noble One until death.
"In this matter, you may act according to your own will regarding what must be done.

After some time had passed and the conversation concerning the description of the single-string necklace had concluded, Rājyaśrī— having gained the confidence of the assembly— summoned her betel-bearer Patralatā and whispered some instruction to her near the king's ear.
Having displayed her humility, Pārvatī addressed the king:
“Your Majesty, the Queen requests: I do not recall ever having spoken even a loud word in the presence of my noble lord; how much less could I have made a formal request?”
For this state, brought on by ill fortune, which renders sorrows unbearable and exerts its influence, loosens one's self-restraint.
For women, generally, their husband or their offspring is their support;
but for those deprived of both, there remains only life itself—which acts as fuel for the fire of suffering—and sheer lack of modesty.
"Furthermore, even though his attempt at death was thwarted by the arrival of the noble one,
let this person, who is not a vessel for merit, be favored by the permission to take up the saffron robes.
Upon hearing this, the lord of men remained silent.
Then the teacher spoke very calmly: “O long-lived one,
grief is indeed a synonym for a demon, another form of despair.”
Youth is the darkness;
it is the specific poison;
the leader of the city of the dead is endless.
This is the fire whose nature is non-extinction;
this is the inexhaustible consumption;
this is the Janārdana who is the abode of misfortune.
This mendicant is one who has set out toward demerit;
this sleep is a state of non-awakening; this feverish affliction possesses the nature of a lack of vigor.
This is Vināyaka, the companion of Aśiva;
this is the host of planets frequented by the ignorant;
this is a type of celestial body arising from inauspicious conjunctions.
From affection arises the provocation of wind;
from mental passion arises the birth of fire;
from a state of moisture arises the agitation of dust.
From passion comes desiccation,
and from attachment comes transformation by time; thus,
for this great wound of the heart that constantly bleeds, there is the entry and expansion of the dense darkness of the defilements.

[These teachings are] illuminated by the lightning-flashes of radiant and faultless knowledge; they are profound in their grasp of the hidden core of dense and complex treatises; they are skilled at destroying the entire host of the great elements for the sake of emptiness—the thief of life, the sovereign of defects who is expert at annihilating all bodily forms, abounding in the afflictions of emaciation, labored breathing, and delirium, a long-lasting disease and a malevolent seizure, a comet portending the destruction of the whole world, expert at seizing away life, devoid of auspicious luster, and falling like a thunderbolt from a cloudless sky.

The hearts of even the learned, hardened by the recitation of many poetic tales and vast with the bearing of numerous branches of knowledge, are not capable of enduring even a sudden onset; how much less so the heart of a young woman, tender as a *navamālikā* flower and as weak as a fresh lotus fiber?
This being the case, O Satyavrata!
Tell me, what is to be done here? Who is to be reproached? Before whom are they to be loudly cried out?
Or is this heart-burning sorrow to be made public?
All of it must be endured with eyes closed by one who is not deluded and who possesses the nature of a mortal.
O virtuous lady, these ancient laws of existence—who is able to alter them?

The exceedingly long ropes of the water-wheel mechanism that fashions birth, old age, and death for all five classes of beings turn day and night; they are skilled in observing the activities of the internal organs presided over by the five great elements and the five families; they are all-devouring, treacherous, and the established laws of the King of Dharma;
and in every dwelling, the water-clocks of Time, expert at calculating the portions of the lifespan, flow away without enduring even for a moment.
In this world, the command of Yama moves swiftly as Caṇḍikā, striking down the life-force of all living beings.
The drums of the Lord of the Dead resound incessantly, skilled in proclaiming the departure of every creature.

Wandering in every direction with their troupes are the agents of Death—men whose eyes are red like heated iron, whose bodies are dark as the hue of the *kālakūṭa* poison, and who carry the nooses of Time in their hands.

In every house, there wander terrifying proclamations of dreadful execution, frightening with the sharp clanging of the bells of Yama struck by the hands of his fearsome servants, intended to summon away the entire multitude of living beings. In every direction flow the streets—highways for the caravan of travelers departing for the dwelling of the next world—where the vultures’ eyes fall sharply upon the banners of the Lord of the Dead, grey with the smoke of many funeral pyres; where they are crowded with thousands of bier-vehicles for corpses, variegated by the tangles of hair scattered by mourning wives amidst a clamor of grief; and where the young jackals in the camps of the cremation grounds howl with cries of "ki-la-ki-la."

The tongue of the Night of Doom—black as the coals of a funeral pyre, smeared with blood, licking the heights of the sky, and greedy for the devouring of the entire world—licks up the lives of living beings.
And the hunger of Death, the Lord who devours all creatures, knows no satiety.
Moreover, the river of impermanence flows with extreme rapidity.
The assemblies of the great elements are momentary;
in the nights, the wooden frames of the bodies of embodied beings—those cages of vessels—are fragile.
Helpless under the influence of the unwholesome and the wholesome, the atoms that constitute the fabrication of the body fall apart.
The cords and threads of the snare that bind living beings are easily severed;
the entire universe is devoid of a sovereign self and is perishable.
Having ascertained this, O wise one, you ought not to allow the expansion of darkness into your tender mind to such an extent.
"Even a single moment of discernment becomes a support for steadfastness.
Moreover, even though your grief has gone far away, surely this eldest brother of yours, who is like a father, remains a venerable elder to you who must now look to him.
Otherwise, who would not highly esteem such a virtuous resolve as yours, made here regarding the taking up of the saffron robes?"
For the blessed state of renunciation is indeed the cause for allaying the fever of the entire mind;
this is truly superior for those who possess the Supreme Self. But now, the illustrious one shatters my heart's desire.

"Whatever he commands must be carried out—whether he addresses one as 'brother,' 'eldest,' 'child,' 'virtuous one,' or 'king'—one must in every way abide by his command. Having said this, he ceased speaking. When he had finished, the king declared: "Who else but my noble brother could speak in such a manner?"
For you are pillars of support for the world during its precarious calamities, fashioned by a providence that requires no solicitation;
you are lamps of Dharma whose forms are moistened with affection, destroying the darkness of delusion.
Yet, those who are spoiled by the granting of favors desire even an unattainable wish out of excessive fondness.

Excessive affection imposes audacity upon the heart of even the steadfast, overstepping its natural modesty; and because they are devoid of discernment between what is proper and improper, thirst for self-interest teaches even the shy man boldness. Yet the noble, like the oceans, maintain the bounds of propriety even when entreated.

Moreover, this body of mine was already offered unasked by you, who are worthy of honor, as hospitality from the very beginning. Therefore, I beg a small favor of the Venerable One: this sister of ours is young and afflicted by many sorrows; she must be constantly cherished, even at the cost of neglecting all other duties. Furthermore, we have made a vow in the presence of the whole world, pledging ourselves to obey the arm of one who is intent on bringing about the destruction of the enemy clan that committed the crime of murdering our brother.
Unable to endure the previous insults and humiliations, they have surrendered themselves to anger;
therefore, let even my noble self employ himself in my service for some time.
Let this body be given to the guest.
From this day forward, until this person has lightened the burden of his vow and consoled the subjects who are distressed by the grief of their father’s death,
[I shall attend] to him with your venerable and righteous discourses.
And by means of instructions that bring about wholesome awakening and have swept away all dust,
by teachings that bestow ethical discipline and tranquility,
and by the manifestations of the Tathāgatas which serve as the cause for the abandonment of the afflictions;
I wish to awaken her as she approaches my side;
for she shall take up the saffron robes along with me once my purpose is accomplished.
And what indeed would great men not bestow upon those who come as supplicants?
"Dadhīca, an ocean of fortitude, fulfilled the purpose of the Lord of the Gods even with his own bones;

and the Lord of Sages, disregarding his own existence out of compassion, how many times has he not given himself to dull-witted beings? Beyond this, you yourselves know much more. Having said this, the king became silent.
The venerable one spoke further: “The worthy do not utter their words twice.
Your virtues have already been accepted by my mind; this bodily offering is for that purpose.
As for the utility of this person, who is otherwise useless, it depends upon those possessed of virtue, whether in a small or a great task.”
Then, being delighted by her thus reciprocated affection, the king stayed there that night; and at dawn,
having dismissed her— satisfied with gifts of garments, ornaments, and other things— he returned with his sister and the preceptor Nirghāta, traveling in stages,
to the camp situated on the banks of the Anujāhnava river after only a few days.
And even as he was recounting to his friends the story of his attainment of royal glory, the sun also crossed the expanse of the sky.

Like a lotus-pond turned tawny by thick mud, the day—beloved of the cakravāka birds—contracted; and the rays of light, scattered abroad, were reddened like the color of fresh blood, resembling sacrificial verses (*yajus*) vomited from the mouth of an enraged Yājñavalkya.
The sun, the thief of sins within his own body, again withdrew the nets of his rays;

and gradually, the sun— resplendent with its thick, rising glow— became like the crest-jewel innate to the binding of the turban on Bhīmasena, having been torn away by the hollow of Vṛkodara’s hands, or like the fierce body-unguent of Aśvatthāman, red as fresh blood.
Tawny with the blood filling the veins of the severed heads of the gods released during the crushing of the city by Rudra, who was intent on giving alms, he resembled the skull-bowl of Brahmā;

like a lake that obstructs the distance, filled with thousands of channels of blood flowing from the hollows of the throats of wicked Kṣatriyas hewn by the axe-blade of Paraśurāma— which was enraged at the slaughter of his father and whetted upon the broad and rugged shoulder-masses of Kārtavīrya— he was smeared with blood scattered by the forceful thrusts of the cage-like talons of the great Garuḍa, which had hidden his hands and feet within the circle of his severed heads.
The sun was dying, like a throat being choked;
it had been reduced to a state of emaciation, like a lump of raw flesh with a reddish core within the sky;

cast out by Dākṣāyaṇī, who was distressed by the delay of the appointed time, it was exceedingly vast, its belly stained by the decoction of boiling blood, like a slope of Mount Sumeru marked by the cooking of sacrificial offerings for the sorcery intended to slay the Asuras.
And like a cauldron belonging to Bṛhaspati,
terrifying with its coating of blood from the bodies of elephants and Dānavas recently torn apart, the expanse of Mahābhairava’s face appeared for a moment.

Then the twilight hour, resembling a Vetāla, shone forth, hanging from clouds as bright as the streaks of the sun’s reflection in the waters of the ocean, appearing as if it had seized a load of raw flesh.

The lord of the waters, whose flowing currents were dyed by the blazing glow of twilight, once again assumed a body as pale-red as the mass of blood from Madhu and Kaiṭabha when they were crushed between the thick thighs of the Ancient Being (Viṣṇu).

And when the time of twilight had concluded, immediately thereafter, his royal glory—thirsting to drink the measureless fame of his lineage—seemed like a cup made of the stone of the Pearl Mountain; and his royal fortune, intent on establishing the Kṛta Yuga, seemed like the impression of the silver seal of the first king’s command.
As if a messenger from Śvetadvīpa had arrived for the king who was set out to conquer all the continents, the night brought forth the white-rayed moon; may there be prosperity!
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Harṣacarita*, composed by the great poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
